title: Children learn to be alone through love, not distance | The Optimist Daily
text:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

There is something that makes adults uneasy about a child playing alone. A kid absorbed in something private at a playground edge, a bedroom door closed for an afternoon. These scenes have a way of triggering concern. Are they OK? Do they need something? Should someone go and join in?

This discomfort runs through a lot of modern parenting culture. Unstructured time has quietly become something to be rescued from. There are classes for every interest, enrichment activities for every age, educational games for every developmental window. Underneath it all sits a low-level worry that a child doing nothing productive is somehow falling behind.

British psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott, writing in 1958, would have found a lot to question in that anxiety. In his paper “The Capacity to Be Alone,” he argued that the ability to be comfortably alone is one of the most important signs of emotional maturity. And more unexpectedly: he argued that it doesn’t begin in isolation at all. It begins through repeated experiences of being alone while a trusted person is nearby.

The child who plays freely, absorbed in some private project while a parent reads across the room, is not thriving in spite of the parent’s presence. They are thriving because of it. The relationship is safe enough that it doesn’t need to be continuously checked. The adult has become a kind of emotional background: reliable, undemanding, there. Over time that reliability moves inward. The child can eventually be alone without the security falling apart, because they have felt it enough times alongside someone real.

We tend to assume independence is built through independence, that children learn to be alone by being left alone. Winnicott runs the other way. The child who can play freely has a secure relationship doing quiet work behind them. They don’t need to keep checking because there is nothing to check.

Our culture has blurred these categories considerably. Loneliness is the painful experience of unmet connection. Solitude is time apart from other people, and whether it feels restorative or oppressive depends on whether it was chosen, whether safety exists somewhere in the background, and whether relationships remain available when you want them.

Research on everyday solitude suggests time alone tends to soften highly aroused emotional states, both positive and negative, creating conditions for quieter thinking. Comfort with being alone also shifts with mood, life stage, and circumstance, regardless of personality type. It isn’t simply an introvert thing.

A child playing at the kitchen table while a parent cooks is not the same as a child who is chronically isolated or ignored. One is solitude inside safety. The other is something different entirely.

For most of human history, being physically alone meant being psychologically alone. That has changed. A person can now sit by themselves in an empty room and fill every corner of their awareness with other people’s voices, opinions, and reactions. The phone comes out almost on its own. A message sends, a feed refreshes, a podcast picks up. Whatever quiet was there is gone in seconds.

Technology didn’t invent the impulse to avoid sitting with ourselves, but it has made the avoidance nearly frictionless. We can know what a former colleague’s cousin thinks about a news story before we’ve formed any view of our own.

Children notice this. They watch adults who are rarely psychologically alone, even when no one else is physically in the room. What they absorb from it matters: whether sitting with one’s own thoughts is something a grown person can tolerate, even welcome. A parent who reads, gardens, makes something, or simply sits without immediately reaching for something to distract themselves is modeling more than they might realize.

There is a version of this insight that can sound like a case for self-sufficiency, the emotionally mature person who never needs reassurance or company. That is not what Winnicott was describing. His theory began with relationship. The person who can be comfortably alone hasn’t reduced their need for others. They have built enough inner security to remain themselves when others aren’t present.

That tends to make relationships easier to be in. When people are frightened of solitude, relationships carry the burden of continuously proving they are real. A slow reply becomes rejection. Disagreement feels like withdrawal. Someone else’s need for space gets taken personally. When people can sit with themselves, there is more room for others to simply be people, with their own thoughts, their own evenings, their own corners of life that don’t include you.

For children, this often plays out in small ways. A parent who doesn’t enter every game. A conversation that doesn’t happen immediately. An interest the child has developed that the adults don’t know the details of. These pockets of unwitnessed experience are not evidence of disconnection. They are often where a private self gets formed. The goal is the ability to move between connection and solitude without either one feeling like a threat, and to trust that the relationship survives the movement.
